investigations.title: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity
investigations.space: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI Grant
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
investigations.hypothesis: Without buoyancy, mixing and heat transfer are reduced, the time-temperature history of the combustion vapors (or particle precursors) and particle trajectories are significantly altered, changing the composition of the smoke. The chemical composition of the burning material also affects the characteristics of the smoke generated.
investigations.approach: The formation and growth of dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) particles in Earth gravity and microgravity environments was simulated. Direct numerical simulation via a Navier-Stokes nodal approach was utlilized. The smoke originates from pyrolysis vapor expelled from a heated sample in a geometry similar to that considered in the SAME experiments. This study considered two cross-flow velocities of sufficiently low speed that buoyancy cannot be neglected in the presence of gravity. Simulations are presented to assess the dependence of particle size distributions on thermophoresis, particle settling, and flow geometry. The final report for this investigation introduces the simulation and modeling methodology, followed by a description of the flow geometry and the parameter space under consideration.The differences in the wake geometry attributable to buoyancy for the lower of two flow speeds was examined.  Instantaneous scalar fields were used to describe particle accumulation and growth in the buoyant and non-buoyant wakes that form downstream of the hot vapor source.
investigations.impacts: Models and tools that characterize particles generated as smoke can be used to ascertain how temperature, gravity, and material properties affect the smoke produced. This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices and prevent fires that can lead to loss of materiel and loss of life.

investigations.title: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis
investigations.space: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), PSI grant
investigations.objective: The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.
investigations.hypothesis: External thermo-convective perturbations (imposed temperature gradients, non-uniform heating, oscillatory/shear inflow) were expected to govern cool-flame ignition, oscillation, transition to hot ignition, and extinction by shifting residence time and scalar dissipation. In microgravity, where buoyancy was suppressed, this forcing was anticipated to dominate transport. A multidimensional, multi-physics CFD model was used to map perturbation-dependent stability boundaries and predict observables for comparison with FLEX data.
investigations.approach:
OpenFOAM was used to develop a 3-D CFD model of n-alkane droplet cool flames in microgravity, coupling variable-density Navier–Stokes flow with low-temperature combustion chemistry, coupled heat and mass transfer, and radiation. Model fidelity was established against ISS FLEX measurements, after which controlled simulations examined three forcing modes (i) convection alone to mimic droplet drift, (ii) imposed heat flux, and (iii) combined convection plus heating applied to both large (1–4 mm) and sub-millimeter (~0.5 mm) droplets.

To accelerate progress, the study began with simplified chemistry and transitioned to reduced mechanisms for parameter sweeps over forcing amplitude and frequency, ambient composition (including ozone-assisted cases), and pressure. From each case, predictive observables were extracted (ignition delay, oscillation frequency and amplitude, stand-off and extinction diameters), and were used to construct stability maps that delineated conditions for cool-flame onset, persistence, and quenching. These maps were reconciled with FLEX observations and were used to guide next-generation test matrices for both large- and small-droplet experiments.
investigations.impacts:
Space Benefits: Potential to improve spacecraft fire-safety modeling by resolving cool-flame/extinction behavior in microgravity; leverages FLEX to define safer operating envelopes/materials.
Earth Benefits: Advances low-temperature combustion understanding relevant to engine knock, efficiency, and emissions; delivers validated CFD tools transferrable to practical combustors.

investigations.title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames
investigations.objective:
By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
    1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
    2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
    3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
    4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
    5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry.
investigations.hypothesis: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.
investigations.approach:
Using the experimental conditions of FLEX flight, a comparative studies of the oxygen concentration effects on the extinction limits of cool flames was conducted using three different numerical modeling schemes, (a) spark-assisted flame propagation of a n-heptane/air mixture, (b) one dimensional freely-propagating dimethyl ether (DME) flames using an arc-length continuation method and (c) simulated cool flame regimes and burning limits at elevated pressure (up to 20 atm) using DME/air mixtures.

Specific research details are outlined in the publication, ''Dynamics of cool flames'' [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pecs.2019.100787]; '' Understanding Cool Flames and Warm Flames'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.proci.2020.09.019] and ''Study of the low-temperature reactivity of large n-alkanes through cool diffusion flame extinction'', [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.combustflame.2017.01.028].
investigations.impacts: Obtaining a fundamental understanding of the warm diffusion flame is particularly relevant to combustion in highly turbulent flow fields and in microgravity environments, owing to the possibility of long residence times. The results showed that the warm flame has a double reaction zone structure and plays a critical role in the transition between cool flames and hot flames. At elevated pressures, it was found that the flammable region of warm flames and cool flames expands due to the increase in low-temperature and intermediate-temperature reactivity with pressure. Since many real engines operate in the 20-40 atm pressure range, therefore, cool flames and warm flames are relevant and important flame regimes for high-pressure near-limit combustion applications. These calculations from this investigation will serve to advance the understanding of near-limit flame dynamics and provide guidance for experimental observation of different flame regimes.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
investigations.space: National Science Foundation (NSF), Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS)
investigations.objective:
1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS).
2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate.
3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations.
4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements.
5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.
investigations.hypothesis:
The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics.
  1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners.
  2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane.
  3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures.
  4. Inverse cool diffusion flames.
  5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames.
investigations.approach: Perform spherical diffusion flame tests aboard the International Space Station. Consider multiple fuels, a range of reactant dilutions, flow rates, and pressures for normal and inverse convection directions. Observe the flames with a broad suite of cameras, radiometers, photomultiplier tubes, and thermocouples.
investigations.impacts: Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. However, this progress is being impeded by the limited understanding of the chemistry of cool flames. Research into cool diffusion flames (whose peak temperatures are 500 – 1000 K) has grown exponentially since they were discovered in 2012.  The measurements performed for this project will help to test and advance cool flame kinetics mechanisms. This should facilitate the development of more efficient internal combustion engines.

investigations.title: Structure and Properties of Pb-Sn and Pb-free Sn-Ag-Cu Solders Produced in Terrestrial vs. Microgravity Environments under Extremes of Elevated and Cryo Temperatures
investigations.sub: Microstructural Characterization, Terrestrial vs Microgravity Effects, Solder Joints
investigations.objective: This study addresses the reliability of solder joints in space by pursuing two principal objectives: (1) Characterization of solder-joint formation under microgravity conditions aboard the International Space Station, specifically examining the impact of suppressed convective flow and buoyancy on 40Pb-60Sn alloys utilized in the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI). (2) Evaluation of the solder’s material and mechanical properties under extreme thermal environments, including elevated and cryogenic temperature exposures characteristic of spaceflight conditions.
investigations.hypothesis: In microgravity environments, fluid dynamics are markedly constrained, predominantly governed by solidification-induced volumetric changes, thermally driven density gradients, and Marangoni convection. This suppression of fluid motion results in diminished mixing, causing voids and gas bubbles to remain entrapped within the solder joint during the solidification process. Such internal porosity critically impairs the solder’s thermal and electrical conductivity, while also compromising the mechanical robustness of the joint. To advance the feasibility of extended space missions, this study seeks to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, observable phenomena, and process parameters that influence the structural and functional integrity of solder joints fabricated under terrestrial and microgravity conditions.
investigations.approach:
The study examined three distinct solder alloys: the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) composition, an off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn formulation, and a lead-free alloy consisting of 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu.
Microstructural characterization was performed on four solder specimens processed in microgravity from the ISSI investigation, one terrestrial ISSI solder, and a freshly fabricated terrestrial 40wt%Pb-60wt%Sn sample. These analyses elucidated the role of suppressed buoyancy and natural convection in void formation within microgravity environments. Evidence of void-induced Marangoni convection influencing microstructure development was demonstrated using wire-feed solder processed in space. The micromechanical response of solders fabricated under both terrestrial and microgravity conditions was further evaluated across a broad thermal range (–157ºC to +121ºC), simulating the conditions encountered externally on the International Space Station. Investigations under cryogenic conditions focused on the β-to-α phase transformation in Sn below 13ºC, examining associated volumetric expansion, internal stress evolution, and the ductile-to-brittle transition phenomena observed in Sn-based alloys. At ambient temperature, the influence of accelerated aging on both microstructural stability and mechanical performance was assessed.
investigations.impacts:
The research presented in this project offers significant contributions across multiple space exploration initiatives:

(i) The project objectives are closely aligned with ongoing NASA initiatives focused on metal joining techniques in reduced gravity environments. The three solder alloys investigated—selected in collaboration with NASA partners, underscoring the relevance of the study to future space exploration efforts, (ii) The findings are expected to inform the design of future experiments responsive to forthcoming NASA proposal calls, including those associated with the Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface, (iii) The insights gained into microgravity fluid behavior and surface tension variation can be extended to a broad range of spaceflight-enabling technologies, such as boiling, heat transfer, combustion, welding, brazing, and soldering. This research enhances the understanding of gravity-driven separation processes—such as gas bubble removal—that must be accomplished via alternative mechanisms in microgravity conditions. (iv) The gravity-level-specific protocols (GLSPs) developed for various soldering configurations serve as practical guidance for future investigations into metal joining techniques under reduced gravity. These protocols may be adopted by scientists and flight personnel for welding, brazing, and soldering applications in spaceflight environments.
